I'm the gleeful owner of a Calico M-951 carbine. It had some problems with light strikes, so I ordered a new striker spring... and hand-loading a 100-round magazine is a pain in the buttocks, so I ordered a speedloader. In April 2015. Yeah, you read that right. April 2015 to January 2016. 9 months. Insert baby joke here. While you can find the guns and major parts - like magazines and rails - from third parties and/or used, there isn't really anywhere else to go to get little fiddly bits, like a specific spring... so I was stuck.

Speedloader

The idea is that you empty a box of 50 rounds gently onto the clear plastic tray, bang-side-up, like so:

Speedloader - open

And then close the contraption around them:

Speedloader - closed

And then you stick the magazine in the hole and turn the crank to fill it up:

Speedloader - doin it's thang

Well, it didn't quite work. The rounds would get stuck just above the teeth that were supposed to catch them and force them down into the magazine. After much poking, prodding, peering, and flashlight-ing, I determined that it was probably because the height of the space for the rounds was a little bit more than the height of the rounds, allowing them to angle slightly off the horizontal and not fall nicely into place.

I hypothesized that flat-tipped rounds would perform better in the speedloader, as they would have a harder time tilting than pointy rounds. Unfortunately, the only flat-tipped rounds I could get my hands on after I was at the range (Remington JHP 9mm, a yellow+green box) were shorter than the pointy ones I brought (Monarch (Academy sports store's house brand) 9mm brass):

Left: Remington 9mm JHP 115gr. Right: Monarch 9mm 115gr

Also, they cost literally more than twice as much.

And while the JHP rounds did work better, they, due to being shorter, still had room to tilt and ended up jamming up the speedloader. In fact, much to my dismay, the Monarch rounds were longer than every other 9mm round I compared them to... So now I've either got to find an even longer pointed round, or just a "normally" extra-long flat-nosed round, if I want to really use the speedloader. Bummer.

Also, I had to lubricate and de-horn the speedloader a bit; it was very rigid and rough.

Striker Spring

With a 100-round magazine, it's really easy to compute the %FTF of the gun - just, the number per magazine that fail to fire! My M-951 was sitting at a frustrating 6% FTF and ~1% double-fire, and I couldn't figure out why. I had a bunch of hypotheses (and aggressive cleaning and dry-lube helped a lot), but none of them fixed the issues - just reduced their prevalence.

Every casing that failed to fire had an imprint on the primer that was noticeably more shallow than on successfully-fired casings. So, I thought maybe something was wrong with the striker spring. I did get this gun used, and it was probably manufactured in the early 1990s, so... maybe it was time for a new one!

Also, it bunched up when compressed in a way that I'd never seen another compression spring bunch:

Old striker spring, compressed

The new striker spring arrived, and... What!?

A spring unlike any other

Top to bottom:

  • Bolt Return Spring
  • Tape Measure
  • Old striker spring
  • New striker spring

I was highly skeptical. So much so that I double-checked my order, what was printed on the invoice, and went back to Calico's online store to see if maybe they sent me some other spring.

Nope. This couldn't be anything other than a striker spring. Maybe the one in my gun at the moment wasn't original? Warily, I put the new spring in place. It bunched up even more than the old one:

New strike spring, compressed

I took it apprehensively to the range with 300 rounds of 9mm...

1.3% FTF (light-strike), not a single double-fire in all 300 rounds.

So, it looks like just like all of the other attempts at fixing this gun up (cleaning, lubing, etc), I made it better, but didn't fix anything. This all seems to support the hypothesis that this gun was just poorly cared-for by its previous owner(s).

I'll probably order a whole new bolt assembly from the factory, and update on how that worked out in 2017...

At the end of the day, though, it was still (six times more, in fact) freakisly fun to pump 100 rounds downrange without having to reload. 3 people asked what (the heck) I was shooting, which always makes me feel warm inside, don't'cha know.
I ordered parts from Calico Light Weapon Systems for my M-951 in April 2015... they finally arrived! Replacement striker spring and speedloader.
